title: Rivalry with other trombonists and Stumpy Brady
summary: Stumpy Brady came to New York to teach him, and he outplayed him after hours at the Rhythm Club.

INTERVIEW WITH JAY C. HIGGINBOTHAM
SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION - HISTORY OF JAZZ
The other trombonists, like - you take a trombonist, O.K., Tricky Sam.
I know he never won but, you were always winning, so how did he feel about you? Did he feel that he could cut you when he played?
I don't think so; I don't think nobody felt like that. Nobody felt like that, nobody.
Did you have a lot of trombonists who would say, "Come on, come on to this jam session. I can play better than you."
Yeah, there was one guy who would do that.

What's his name? He's dead now. George Stevens - I don't think you know him. George Stevens. Oh yeah, another one, he's living now but he's not playing. He wrote me a letter. He's with Zack Whyte's band in Cincinnati and he was coming to New York. His name was Stumpy Brady. You know him.

He wrote me a letter. He said, I'm going to come to New York and teach you how to play. So we met in the Savoy after we got through and went to the Rhythm Club. So I wasn't showing off, just took out the horn and started playing ... There wasn't nobody there playing but him. They left him in there by himself.
